Simply clean the surface and apply a new thin coat of wax or a maintenance product recommended by the manufacturer.
With this periodic maintenance, the project can retain its appearance and protection for many years to come.
Wood is a living material.
Even after being processed and finished, it continues to react to the surrounding environment.
It is precisely this characteristic that gives it the charm and uniqueness that synthetic materials cannot replicate.
The result of this stage
At the end of this stage, we should have a project that is fully finished, protected, and ready for use.

Whether you’ve chosen a finish that forms a protective film or an oil- and wax-based system, the goal is the same: to highlight the wood’s natural beauty and provide protection that will allow the project to be used and enjoyed for many years to come.

chapters.title: Finishing projects where wood remains exposed

blocks.text: Working with epoxy resin does not require an industrial workshop or very expensive equipment. Many of the projects presented in this book can be completed with a relatively small set of tools and equipment.
The list below serves as a starting point for those who want to get started.
Measuring and preparation equipment
• precision digital scale;
• containers for mixing the resin;
• spatulas and stirring sticks;
• resin mixer (optional, depending on the quantities being prepared).
Woodworking Tools
• circular saw or jigsaw;
• hand-held router;
• belt sander;
• orbital sander;
• vacuum cleaner.
Assembly Equipment
• clamps;
• screwdriver or power screwdriver;
• ruler, tape measure, and set square;
• level.
Supplies
• sandpaper in various grits;
• adhesive tape;
• silicone for sealing the formwork;
• nitrile gloves;
• lint-free cloths.
Protective Equipment
• safety goggles;
• a respirator suitable for vapors and particles, appropriate for the products being used;
• protective gloves;
• work clothes.

As experience grows and projects become more complex, every builder will expand their workshop with equipment tailored to their own work style. However, it is not necessary to have all of this equipment available from the very first project.
I’ll wrap up this post with a few ideas that don’t come from manufacturers’ manuals or resin data sheets.
These are things I’ve learned in the workshop—sometimes after many hours of work, other times after making mistakes I’d rather not have made.
Never try to rush the resin. Almost every time I've tried to save time, I've ended up spending more time fixing what went wrong.
Planning is one of the most important stages of a project. An hour spent properly preparing the materials, formwork, and work steps can save many hours of corrections.
Don’t rush to use the wood as soon as you buy it. Wood has its own rhythm and needs time to settle. Allowing for this process means fewer surprises later on.

Learn to view each step as a foundation for the next. Careful sanding will make the finishing process easier. A well-planned pour will minimize the need for corrections. Almost every step influences what comes next.

Don’t try to achieve perfection on the first try. Every project will teach you something new, and every mistake will give you experience. The important thing is to understand why it happened and not to repeat it.
Use high-quality materials, but don’t rely solely on them. Even the best resin can’t make up for a sloppy preparation.
Take care of your workshop. Cleanliness, order, and organization are just as important as the tools you use.
And, perhaps most importantly, enjoy the process.

Epoxy resin and wood offer the opportunity to create unique objects. Every piece of wood has its own story, its own shapes, and its own imperfections. It is precisely these qualities that make each project different.
Don’t try to fight the nature of wood. Learn to work with it.

chapters.title: What I've Learned After Years of Working with Epoxy Resin

blocks.text: You have reached the end of this manual.
If you’ve gone through all the chapters and understood the logic behind each step, you already have all the information you need to complete your first project.
Don't try to build the most spectacular resin table you've seen online on your first try.
Start with simple projects.
Give it a try.
Observe how different types of wood react, how the resin behaves, and how each decision influences the final result.
Experience isn’t gained in a day, nor by reading a single book. It is built up project by project.
I hope the information in this manual provides you with a solid starting point and shortens the path that many of us have traveled through trial and error and experience gained over time.
I hope that each project is better than the last and, above all, that you enjoy the creative process.
Good luck!
